t:
Section 20 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. 78t) is amended—

    (1) 

by striking the section heading and inserting the following:

“liability of controlling persons and persons who aid and abet violations”;

and

 
    (2) 
by adding at the end the following new subsection:


“(f) 
Prosecution of Persons Who Aid and Abet Violations.—For purposes of any action brought by the Commission under paragraph (1) or (3) of section 21(d), any person that knowingly provides substantial assistance to another person in violation of a provision of this title, or of any rule or regulation issued under this title, shall be deemed to be in violation of such provision to the same extent as the person to whom such assistance is provided.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to an "action" and to "any rule or regulation issued under this title" signal litigation rights or rulemaking. That fails because the provision only extends liability to aiders and abettors in enforcement actions brought by the SEC, a federal agency, and merely mentions existing rules without granting rulemaking authority. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue over a federal decision.
fable.s: For purposes of any action brought by the Commission under paragraph (1) or (3) of section 21(d), any person that knowingly provides substantial assistance to another person in violation of a provision of this title, or of any rule or regulation issued under this title, shall be deemed to be in violation of such provision

opus.w: This section makes people who aid and abet violations liable in SEC enforcement actions. Only the Commission, a federal agency, brings these actions. No consultation, hearing, comment period, advisory body or new rulemaking authority is created. The mention of an existing "rule or regulation" and of legal "action" is tempting, but neither one gives outside parties a role in a federal decision or a right to challenge one.
opus.s: For purposes of any action brought by the Commission under paragraph (1) or (3) of section 21(d), any person that knowingly provides substantial assistance to another person in violation of a provision of this title, or of any rule or regulation issued under this title, shall be deemed to be in violation of such provision

qwen_chat.w: This section defines legal liability for aiding and abetting securities violations. It does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with any outside parties before making a decision. It does not establish an advisory committee, public hearing, or comment period. The interaction described is between private parties (the aider and the violator), not between the government and an outside party in the context of a federal decision-making process.
qwen_chat.s: any person that knowingly provides substantial assistance to another person in violation of a provision of this title, or of any rule or regulation issued under this title, shall be deemed to be in violation of such provision to the same extent as the person to whom such assistance is provided
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "aiding and abetting" implies some form of interaction or coordination with the violator, which could be misconstrued as participation. However, this is a substantive liability provision defining who is legally responsible for violations, not a procedural requirement for the government to consult with outsiders before making a decision. The section does not require the SEC to consult with anyone, nor does it grant outsiders a right to participate in the decision-making process. It simply expands the scope of who can be prosecuted.
